questiontext.text:
Goal

You write four functions that change a job queue in place and sort a list of sites two ways.

How this works in Python

Java gives a list one of two personalities depending on how you built it.

List<String> jobs = new ArrayList<>(List.of("scan", "flush"));
jobs.add("upload");                    // fine, an ArrayList changes

List<String> fixed = List.of("scan", "flush");
fixed.add("upload");                   // UnsupportedOperationException at run time

Collections.sort(jobs);                                  // sorts jobs itself, returns void
List<String> fresh = jobs.stream().sorted().toList();    // new list, jobs untouched

Python has one list and it always changes. A list literal such as ["scan", "flush"] has no read-only cousin, so nothing here throws UnsupportedOperationException. The fixed sequence Python does have arrives later in the course.

Changing an object where it stands, rather than building a new one, is called mutating it. The change happens in place, so every name pointing at that list sees the result. These five list methods all mutate.

  • jobs.append(x) adds one item to the end.
  • jobs.extend(other) adds every item of another list to the end.
  • jobs.insert(0, x) puts x at position 0 and shifts the rest right.
  • jobs.remove(x) removes the first item whose value equals x. Java's List.remove(1) removes the item sitting at index 1, so read this one twice.
  • jobs.pop() removes the last item and returns it. jobs.pop(0) removes and returns the first.

Four of those five return None, which is Python's null. Only pop hands anything back, because it is the only one with something to give. That convention runs through the whole language. A method that mutates returns nothing.

Sorting shows the split most clearly, because Python spells the two halves of Collections.sort and stream().sorted() with two names that look almost identical.

sites = ["Taupo", "Kaikoura", "Napier"]

fresh = sorted(sites)      # a function. Returns a new sorted list and leaves sites alone
print(sites)               # ['Taupo', 'Kaikoura', 'Napier']

sites.sort()               # a method. Sorts sites itself and returns None
print(sites)               # ['Kaikoura', 'Napier', 'Taupo']

The trap is one line long.

sites = sites.sort()       # sites now holds None

Nothing complains. The name sites holds None, and the sorted list has been thrown away. Python reports the mistake several lines later, when something calls a list method on None and raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'index'. The traceback, which is Python's stack trace, points at that innocent later line rather than at the assignment that caused the problem.

Your task

Write four functions.

  • load_queue(jobs, arrivals) changes jobs in place and returns nothing. Add the string calibrate at the end, then add every item of arrivals at the end, then put the string power_on at the front. In that order.
  • clear_one(jobs, unwanted) removes the first item equal to unwanted, then removes the last item and returns it.
  • ranked(sites) returns a new sorted list and leaves the caller's list as it found it.
  • rank_here(sites) sorts the caller's list in place and returns whatever the method hands back. The test prints that value on purpose.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Change the list you were given. Build no new list inside load_queue or clear_one.
  • Make every change with the five methods above. No +=, no del, and no assigning to a slice.
  • Never write sites = sites.sort(). Meet that line here and never type it again.
  • Write no loop, and do not call len().
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: queue = ["scan", "flush", "scan", "purge"] print(clear_one(queue, "scan")) print(queue) sites = ["Taupo", "Kaikoura", "Napier"] print(ranked(sites)) print(sites) print(rank_here(sites)) print(sites)

import inspect loader = inspect.getsource(load_queue) clearer = inspect.getsource(clear_one) whole = loader + clearer + inspect.getsource(ranked) + inspect.getsource(rank_here) assert "for " not in whole and "while " not in whole, "rule broken: the methods do the work, write no loop" assert "len(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not call len()" assert "+=" not in whole and "del " not in whole, "rule broken: use the five methods" assert "return" not in loader, "rule broken: load_queue changes the list and returns nothing" assert ".append(" in loader and ".extend(" in loader and ".insert(" in loader, "rule broken: append, extend, insert" assert ".remove(" in clearer and ".pop(" in clearer, "rule broken: remove then pop" assert "sorted(" in inspect.getsource(ranked), "rule broken: ranked returns a new list from sorted()" assert "sorted(" not in inspect.getsource(rank_here), "rule broken: rank_here calls the .sort() method" assert ".sort()" in inspect.getsource(rank_here), "rule broken: rank_here calls the .sort() method" assert "= sites.sort()" not in whole, "rule broken: that line throws the sorted list away" lost = rank_here(["delta", "alpha"]) print(lost is None) try: print(lost.index("alpha")) except AttributeError as problem: print("AttributeError:", problem) solo = ["only"] load_queue(solo, []) print(solo) print(clear_one(solo, "power_on")) print(solo)

expected.text: True AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'index' ['power_on', 'only', 'calibrate'] calibrate ['only']

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write three functions that tidy, rotate and sort a list of readings without touching the caller's copy.

How this works in Python

Java sorts a list two ways and both of them read clearly at the call site.

List<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<>(readings);
Collections.sort(copy);                              // in place, returns void
List<Integer> fresh = readings.stream().sorted().toList();   // new list

Python splits the same pair across two names that look almost identical.

  • sorted(readings) is a function. It returns a new sorted list and leaves readings as it found it.
  • readings.sort() is a method. It sorts readings itself and returns None.

None is Python's null. Write best = readings.sort() and the line runs without complaint. Three lines later best.count(5) raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'count'. The traceback, which is Python's stack trace, points at that later line rather than at the assignment that caused the problem. Python returns None from every list method that changes the list in place.

These are the list methods this exercise needs.

  • readings.append(x) adds one item to the end.
  • readings.extend(other) adds every item of another list to the end.
  • readings.insert(0, x) puts x at position 0 and shifts the rest right.
  • readings.remove(x) removes the first item equal to x and raises ValueError when there is none.
  • readings.pop() removes the last item and returns it. pop(0) removes and returns the first.
  • readings.index(x) returns the position of the first item equal to x.
  • readings.count(x) returns how many items equal x.
  • x in readings is True when x appears at least once.

One of those methods is a trap for a Java developer. Java's List.remove(1) removes the item at index 1. Python's readings.remove(1) removes the first item whose value is 1. Same spelling, different job.

remove deletes one item per call. To delete every occurrence of a value, keep calling it while the value is still present. Python writes a while loop with no brackets around the test and no braces around the body. The indented lines below the header are the body.

while 5 in work:
    work.remove(5)

One idea here matters more than the rest. A function that changes a list its caller still holds has changed the caller's data. Copy the list first with readings[:] from the slicing topic, work on the copy, and return the copy.

Your task

Write three functions.

  • tidy(readings, drop) returns a new sorted list. Every item equal to drop is gone, and the two calibration bounds 0 and 100 are added. The caller's list is unchanged when you return.
  • rotate(readings) returns a new list where the last item has moved to the front and everything else has shifted right. The caller's list is unchanged.
  • sort_result(readings) returns whatever .sort() hands back when you call it on a copy. The test prints that value on purpose.

The tests print the caller's list after each call, so an in-place method on the parameter fails them.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Leave the caller's list exactly as you found it. Call no changing method on the parameter itself.
  • Do not write a for loop. The list methods, in, while and sorted() are enough.
  • Do not call len().
  • Print the None from sort_result on purpose. Meeting it by accident three lines later is the failure this exercise prevents.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (tidy, rotate, sort_result)) assert "for " not in whole, "rule broken: no for loop" assert "len(" not in whole, "rule broken: do not call len()" assert "readings.append(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "readings.remove(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "readings.extend(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "readings.insert(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "readings.sort(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "readings.pop(" not in whole, "rule broken: leave the caller's list alone" assert "sorted(" in inspect.getsource(tidy), "rule broken: tidy must use sorted()" original = [9, 4, 9, 1] snapshot = original[:] tidy(original, 9) rotate(original) sort_result(original) print(original == snapshot) print(original.count(9), original.index(4), 9 in original, 7 in original)

questiontext.text:
Goal

You write five functions that build grids, empty lists in place, rebind a parameter, and copy a nested structure.

How this works in Python

Java passes references by value, and so does Python. Reassign a parameter inside a method and the caller sees nothing. Change the object the parameter points at and the caller sees everything. You already know this rule. Python developers break it for the same reason Java developers do. Reassigning a parameter and changing the object it points at look almost the same on the page.

void replace(List<int[]> batches) { batches = new ArrayList<>(); }  // caller unaffected
void wipe(List<int[]> batches)    { batches.clear(); }              // caller sees empty

Python has no new, so nothing on the page tells you a copy happened. Assignment in Python never copies. A name is a label tied to an object, and b = a ties a second label to the same object.

a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3]

Copying is a separate act. readings[:] from the slicing topic makes a shallow copy, which is a new outer list holding the same inner objects. new ArrayList<>(old) in Java is shallow in exactly the same way. When the items are themselves lists, both copies still share those lists.

Now the trap that survives your tests. In Java, new int[3][3] allocates three separate rows. The Python spelling that looks the same does not.

grid = [[0] * 3] * 3        # looks like three rows
grid[0][0] = 9
print(grid)                 # [[9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0], [9, 0, 0]]

The inner [0] * 3 builds one row. The outer * 3 then stores three references to that one row. Write one cell and you write all three, because there is only one row. A test that checks grid[0][0] == 9 passes, which is why this bug reaches production.

Do not type that expression in this exercise. Build the sharing by hand instead, so you can see what the star was doing.

To copy a nested structure properly, the standard library has copy.deepcopy. It walks the whole structure and rebuilds every level.

import copy
deep = copy.deepcopy(records)

One function below needs a loop. Where Java writes for (int[] batch : batches), Python writes for batch in batches:. There are no brackets around the header and no braces around the body. The indented lines below the header are the body.

Your task

Write five functions.

  • shared_grid() returns a three-by-three grid of zeros where all three rows are the same list object. Bind one row to a name, then put that name in the outer list three times.
  • independent_grid() returns a three-by-three grid of zeros where the three rows are three separate lists.
  • wipe(batches) empties every inner list so the caller sees empty lists afterwards. It returns nothing. batch.clear() empties a list in place.
  • replace(batches) binds the parameter name to a brand-new list [[9, 9]] and returns it. The caller's list stays as it was, which is the point of the function.
  • shallow_and_deep(records) returns two copies of records. The shallow copy first, then the deep copy. Return them as one bare comma-separated expression.

The tests change an item through each copy and then print the original, so only a real deep copy passes the last test.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not use * to repeat a row. Build the sharing by hand so you can see what it shares.
  • Never fix a mutating function by rebinding its parameter. Rebinding is invisible to the caller.
  • Import copy only once you can say out loud why a shallow copy cannot do the job.
  • Write no loop inside independent_grid. Three list literals, typed out.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: grid = shared_grid() print(grid) grid[0][0] = 9 print(grid) print(grid[0] is grid[1]) good = independent_grid() good[0][0] = 9 print(good) print(good[0] is good[1])

import inspect whole = "".join(inspect.getsource(f) for f in (shared_grid, independent_grid, wipe, replace, shallow_and_deep)) assert "* 3" not in whole and "*3" not in whole and "] *" not in whole, "rule broken: no star repetition for rows" assert "for " not in inspect.getsource(independent_grid), "rule broken: three literals, no loop" assert "batches =" not in inspect.getsource(wipe), "rule broken: rebinding is not a fix" assert "deepcopy(" in whole, "rule broken: a shallow copy cannot do the job" original = [["a"], ["b"]] shallow, deep = shallow_and_deep(original) shallow[0].append("x") deep[1].append("y") print(original) print(shallow) print(deep) print(shallow[0] is original[0], deep[0] is original[0])
